newsitem.title: UK: Dollar hits multi-year high on mark, yen in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dollar hits multi-year high on mark, yen in Europe.

text.p: The dollar hit multi-year highs against the mark and yen on Friday, its energy unleashed by a growing notion that leading nations will not try to shoot it down at their meeting this weekend.

Analysts saw no reason why the dollar should not keep its strong tone throughout the day after topping 1.6600 marks, a level not seen since mid-June 1994, and rising above 124 yen to its highest in four years.

But the market was loath to push the dollar much higher ahead of U.S. employment data -- which showed U.S. jobs rose 271,000 in December -- and the meeting of Group of Seven finance ministers and central bank governors to be held in Berlin this weekend, they said.

"There's enough in the pipeline to make people think it's worth sitting and waiting, although you wouldn't expect what we've seen to fall," said Francis Breedon, foreign exchange economist at Lehman Brothers.
The dollar was at 1.6635 marks at Europe's midday, off its high of 1.6645 but more than a pfenning above its late Thursday levels.
Against the yen, it was just below its four-year peak of 124.40, up from its late Thursday level of 123.83.
The dollar got a boost early in the day from German Finance Minister Theo Waigel's comment that there was no sense in trying to set currency targets at this weekend's G7 meeting in Berlin.
Waigel told the Die Welt newspaper in an interview on Friday: "You can't determine exchange rates with statements. No movement can be achieved against the market with communiques."

In the run-up to the G7 meeting, there seemed to be some doubt among the authorities about the ability of governments and central banks to go against the markets, said Adrian Davies, senior strategist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull.
Earlier this week, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said the dollar was unlikely to be lowered through international cooperation.

The market would likely steer clear of pushing the dollar much higher for now for fear it would provoke the G7, currently expected to stick to non-committal comments about foreign exchange, into making hard-hitting comments, analysts said.
"If we get a volatile day today, it would put a lot more urgency into the G7 meeting. That might increase the probability of their coming out with something more serious," Lehman's Breedon said.

Germany, meanwhile, announced on Thursday said the number of its unemployed in January rose by more than half a million, on an unadjusted basis, to a post-war record of 4.66 million. Japan is haunted by a prolonged economic slump, anaemic stock market and ailing banking sector.

From the technical viewpoint, analysts said the dollar was eyeing the psychologically important 125 yen level, although it was seen capped at 124.50 for the day. Against the mark, chartists said the 1.66 marks level, although already tested, would continue to provide a tough short-term barrier.
